records.place: Loreto Aprutino, province of Pescara, Trebbiano d'Abruzzo DOC, Abruzzo

wine.name: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo
wine.classification: DOC, recognised for Trebbiano d'Abruzzo in 1972
wine.grapes: Trebbiano Abruzzese, the region's own Trebbiano, rather than the Trebbiano Toscano that the rule also allows.
wine.sites: The family's hillside vineyards around Loreto Aprutino, inland from Pescara and within reach of the Adriatic; only part of the crop is ever bottled under the family name.
wine.making: Aged in large old oak casks rather than small barrels, then released late, when the house judges it ready. Only the lots the family accepts are bottled, the rest of the crop is sold, and in some years no Trebbiano is released at all. The house says little of its methods.
wine.glass: Smoke, yellow apple and hay over salted lemon when young, turning waxy and nutty with age; full in texture yet dry and saline, with fresh, steady acidity and a savoury finish that lingers.
wine.ageing: It opens slowly over its first years in bottle and, from a sound cellar, can live for decades.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool but not cold; open a young bottle an hour ahead or decant it; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The region's white DOC, recognised in 1972, of at least 85 per cent Trebbiano Abruzzese or Trebbiano Toscano.
Italy's controlled designation of origin, the tier below DOCG; Trebbiano d'Abruzzo has no DOCG.

records.table: In large old casks at Loreto Aprutino, the family's hillside fruit becomes Valentini's Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, bottled only in the years the house accepts. Smoky, saline and slow to open, it shows how long a Trebbiano can live; pour it cool but not cold.
records.story: Since the seventeenth century, by one account from 1650, the Valentini family has held land at Loreto Aprutino, in the hills inland from Pescara. Its modern story is that of Edoardo Valentini, who died in 2006. In the 1950s he gave up a career in the law to return to the family estate, and set out to prove that Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, a name known mostly for plain white wine, could give a white of depth that lasts for decades. He sold most of the crop, a habit the house has kept, and bottled only the lots he judged worthy, so that in some years no Trebbiano appeared at all. He worked in large old casks rather than small new barrels, spoke little of his methods, and the estate's reticence became part of its story. In 1972 Trebbiano d'Abruzzo became a DOC, a name that came to cover much plain white wine, and Valentini's bottle is the one teachers reach for to show what the same name can hold. After his death his son ran the estate along the same lines. Anyone who judges a wine by its grape or its appellation should taste this Trebbiano: a humble name, and a white that lives for decades.

others.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
others.note: The house's red, structured and long lived, and like the white not made in every vintage.

others.name: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
others.note: The house's rosato of Montepulciano, given the same patient treatment as the red and the white.

traps: Valentini of Loreto Aprutino is not La Valentina, a different Abruzzo estate that also bottles Trebbiano d'Abruzzo.
Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a DOC, not a DOCG, and the vine behind Valentini's wine is Trebbiano Abruzzese, not Trebbiano Toscano.
A missing year in a run of Valentini is the house's choice, not a gap in the list: not every vintage is released.

cards.front: Which Trebbiano grows at Loreto Aprutino for Valentini's Trebbiano d'Abruzzo?
cards.back: Trebbiano Abruzzese, the region's own vine, rather than the Trebbiano Toscano the DOC also allows.

cards.front: Who made Valentini's name, and in which decade did he return to the family estate?
cards.back: Edoardo Valentini, who gave up the law in the 1950s and died in 2006.

questions.q: A guest notices that a vintage of Valentini's Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is missing from the list. What lies behind the gap?
opts: It bottles only the lots and years it accepts
Its DOC forbids any release in cool years
The wine is sold only after ten years
Its vines are replanted every few years
questions.exp: The house sells most of its crop and bottles only the lots it judges worthy, so some vintages never appear; no rule of the DOC forbids a release in a cool year.

questions.q: Before he turned his family's Loreto Aprutino estate towards bottled Trebbiano in the 1950s, which career did Edoardo Valentini give up?
opts: The law
Medicine
Banking
Architecture
questions.exp: He left a career in law to return to the family estate and made the house's name until his death in 2006; no account gives him a career in medicine.

report: Searches for this record: 7 in the author's first run (the group's 33 of the share of 35, three shared on the appellations, one fetch of emidiopepe.com refused) and 4 in the second run's read-through (the group's 12 of a fresh share of 35). Valentini has no site the search reached, so the record rests on the library, WineNews, Vinous, two merchants' pages and the consorzio's disciplinare.

The grape: Vinous's vertical (an older biotype of Trebbiano Abruzzese, kept by massal selection), Decanter's piece on where to find Trebbiano (the Abruzzese, not the Toscano) and the Wine Scholar Guild (Valentini among the reference wines of Trebbiano Abruzzese) agree; Decanter's producer profile gave way to Vinous in the sources for the cap. The ministry's consolidated disciplinare gives at least 85 per cent Trebbiano Abruzzese or Trebbiano Toscano, and the 1972 text named Trebbiano d'Abruzzo (Bombino bianco); the label's means now says at least 85 per cent.

Edoardo Valentini's death in 2006 is in WineNews (30 April 2006) and Fine and Rare Wines (at 72), but no source read gives his birth year, 1933 or 1934 by that age (a search of the second run found none either), so he carries his death alone. Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Francesco Paolo Valentini, his wife Elena Valentini and their son Gabriele Valentini.

The roots in Loreto Aprutino from 1650 are WineNews's, and Fine and Rare Wines says since the 1600s, hence the seventeenth century; the first commercial vintage of 1956 is Fine and Rare Wines' alone and is left as the 1950s. The law career rests on Fine and Rare Wines and IT Wine Club.

The plan's why (old pergola vines) and the region record (the two estates that keep their tendone) speak of pergola, and in the first run two searches found no source that says so of Valentini's own vineyards; in the second, a search summary of Vinous's vertical spoke of the pergola abruzzese, a single source, so training is still left out for the refuter. Decanter speaks of tendone in Abruzzo at large.

vino.com's sheets for 2018 and 2020 give fermentation with native yeasts in large casks, about a year in casks of 50 and 70 hectolitres and bottling without filtration, and Scatti di Gusto says no barrique, only large casks; one merchant's two pages are not two sources, so the making keeps the library's large old wood and late release, and the refuter may settle the rest.
The soil (sandy, calcareous clay) is Fine and Rare Wines' alone and is left out; the share of vintages released (about seven in ten) is one merchant's and is left out.
La Valentina, the trap's other estate, is a different producer whose Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is listed by two merchants (Dalla Terra, Superiore.de); no library record is in tension with this one.

open: Training is still left out of the sites: the pergola abruzzese is now on Vinous's vertical (the author's reading) and on two Italian merchants' pages the refuter read (Enoteca Gambi, Pedrelli), which would be two sources, but the record's five sources are full and the field reads true without it; the integrator may add it.
Edoardo Valentini's birth year is still in no source read: Fine and Rare Wines gives his death in 2006 at 72, so 1933 or 1934, and he keeps his death alone.
The ageing in large casks is about a year on two merchants' pages and six to twelve months on another; the record gives no length, which stands.

records.place: Torano Nuovo, province of Teramo, Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC, Abruzzo

wine.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, from the family's own vineyards around Torano Nuovo.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the hills of Torano Nuovo in the north of Abruzzo, where the house began on a small plot in 1964; many vines are trained on the traditional pergola and farmed organically and biodynamically.
wine.making: The Montepulciano is destemmed by hand, rubbed over a net on a wooden vat so the berries fall through and the stems stay behind, then fermented in glass lined cement tanks, some in use since 1964. It ages in cement, with no wood at all, is bottled unfiltered and then rests in the house's cellar, often for many years before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, black cherry and dried plum with blood orange peel, wild herbs and a smoky, tarry note; of medium to full weight, with lively acidity, grippy tannin that softens to silk over the years, and no taste of oak.
wine.ageing: Fierce when young and built for the long haul: the house keeps a deep library of old vintages and releases some of them decades after the harvest.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead and an old one gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The region's red DOC; Montepulciano is the grape here, not the Tuscan town.
Italy's controlled designation of origin, the tier the house's red carries.

records.table: Hand destemmed at Torano Nuovo, then fermented and aged in glass lined cement with no wood and bottled unfiltered, Emidio Pepe's Montepulciano d'Abruzzo tastes of sour cherry, blood orange and wild herbs. Old vintages, decanted once by the house before release, are decanted again, gently, at the table.
records.story: Bulk sales were the rule for the wine the Pepe family made at Torano Nuovo, in the hills of Teramo, from 1899 by its own account. Emidio Pepe (1932 to 2026), born into that farming family, began bottling under his own name in 1964, starting with a small plot near the village and the glass lined cement tanks the cellar has used ever since. From the start he worked by hand: the red grapes destemmed over a net, the white Trebbiano trodden by foot in wooden tubs, no oak at all. Rather than sell every vintage young, the family kept back part of each harvest in its cellar, and before an old vintage of the red leaves the house each bottle is decanted by hand off its sediment into a new bottle, topped up from a second bottle of the same year and closed with a new cork printed with the year of decanting. His daughters and then his granddaughters worked beside him, and he died on 28 July 2026, aged 94. Slowness is the lesson of the house: Montepulciano with no wood, years in the cellar, released when it is judged ready.

others.name: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo
others.note: The house's white, its grapes trodden by foot in wooden tubs; with Valentini's, the long lived Trebbiano a candidate is expected to know.

others.name: Pecorino
others.note: A revived white grape of Abruzzo bottled on its own; the wine is no relation of the sheep's milk cheese of the same name.

traps: Pepe's Montepulciano sees no oak: fermentation and ageing are in glass lined cement, so a toasty, vanilla note in a blind wine argues against it.
Only the white Trebbiano is trodden by foot; the Montepulciano is destemmed by hand over a net.
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is named for its grape; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is the Sangiovese of the Tuscan town.

cards.front: Which vessels does Emidio Pepe ferment and age its Montepulciano in?
cards.back: Glass lined cement tanks, some in use since 1964, with no wood at all.

cards.front: What does the house do to an old vintage of Emidio Pepe before it is released?
cards.back: Each bottle is decanted by hand off its sediment into a new one, topped up from a second bottle of the same year and given a new cork printed with the year.

questions.q: How does Emidio Pepe handle its Montepulciano grapes before fermentation?
opts: Destemmed by hand over a net on a wooden vat
Trodden by foot with their stems in wooden tubs
Crushed by machine and chilled for a week
Fermented as whole bunches in small oak barrels
questions.exp: The house destems the Montepulciano by hand over a net so the berries fall through; treading by foot in wooden tubs is kept for the white Trebbiano.

questions.q: Emidio Pepe first bottled the family's wine under his own name in which year?
questions.exp: The first bottle with the Emidio Pepe label was of 1964; 1899 is when the family began making wine, by its account, and 1932 the year of his birth.

sources.title: Emidio Pepe: the artisanal method
Emidio Pepe: 1964 to 2024, the cellar turns sixty
Noble Rot, reprinted by the estate: Emidio Pepe and the road less travelled
Gambero Rosso: the death of Emidio Pepe and the legacy of his wine
Sky TG24: Emidio Pepe, Abruzzo winegrower, dies at 94

report: Searches for this record: 5 in the author's first run, where the one fetch of the group, the house's method page, was refused (emidiopepe.com does not resolve here), and 1 in the second run; the house's own pages were read through search.

The plan's note is answered: Emidio Pepe died at home at Torano Nuovo on 28 July 2026, aged 94, a day after his birthday (Sky TG24, Gambero Rosso, Wine Spectator, Wein.plus), and the Noble Rot profile gives his birth in 1932, so he is named with his dates.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: his daughters Sofia Pepe and Daniela Pepe, his granddaughters Chiara De Iulis Pepe and Elisa De Iulis Pepe; his wife, named by one merchant, is not named for want of her status.

Library tension: p-emidio-pepe's style says the grapes are crushed by foot, and the region record says one Teramo estate crushes by foot; the house's own method page says the Montepulciano is destemmed by hand over a net and only the Trebbiano is trodden by foot in a wooden tub, which the record follows.
The library's founded 1964 is kept: the house dates the family's winemaking to 1899, by the founder's grandfather of the same name, and its first labelled bottle to 1964.

The time in cement (24 months by Vinous, 18 to 24 by the Noble Rot profile, two years by a merchant) is left as ages in cement, and the fermentation's length (eight days, ten to twelve, twenty eight to thirty) disagrees and is left out. Bottled unfiltered now rests on the house's own decanting sheet (Epoca di decantazione, emidiopepe.com, 2022: the founder chose to age his wines without ever filtering them) and the Noble Rot profile; the sheet is not in the sources for the cap of five.

Left out for one source or disagreement: the parcels Casa Pepe (planted 1974) and Branella (1966), the Montepulciano selection the house traces to 1890, and the age past which old bottles are decanted (the house's sheet says the wait was lengthened from ten years to twenty, so the record gives no figure); the Noble Rot profile's bottling without sulphur is against the house's present label, which lists sulphites, and is left out.

changed: story: "From the start he held that Montepulciano d'Abruzzo could make one of the great reds of Italy, and he made it by hand:"; now "From the start he worked by hand:": the founder's belief rests on no source of the refuter's and reads as a judgement of rank; the hand work that follows stands on the house's method page and Vinous.

story: "before an old vintage leaves the house each bottle is opened, decanted off its sediment, topped up from a second bottle of the same year and corked again, the year of decanting printed on the cork."; now "before an old vintage of the red leaves the house each bottle is decanted by hand off its sediment into a new bottle, topped up from a second bottle of the same year and closed with a new cork printed with the year of decanting.": the house's decanting sheet (Epoca di decantazione, 2022) and its method page pour the wine from the old bottle into a new one, top it up from a second bottle of the same vintage and close it with a new cork bearing the year; the sheet also says the Trebbiano is never decanted, so the old vintage is the red's.

story: "His daughters and then a granddaughter worked beside him, and he died at Torano Nuovo on 28 July 2026, a day after his ninety fourth birthday."; now "His daughters and then his granddaughters worked beside him, and he died on 28 July 2026, aged 94.": Sky TG24 gives the daughters at the helm for twenty years with the granddaughters beside them, plural; the death on 28 July 2026 at 94 is in Sky TG24, Adnkronos and Vinous, but the birthday the day before and the place of death are in no source of the refuter's, so they go.

cards[1].back: "Each bottle is decanted off its sediment, topped up from a bottle of the same year and corked again, the year of decanting printed on the cork."; now "Each bottle is decanted by hand off its sediment into a new one, topped up from a second bottle of the same year and given a new cork printed with the year.": the same correction as the story, on the house's decanting sheet; the front is unchanged, so the card keeps its id.

others[1].note: "A revived white grape of Abruzzo bottled on its own; the name has nothing to do with the cheese."; now "A revived white grape of Abruzzo bottled on its own; the wine is no relation of the sheep's milk cheese of the same name.": the grape and the cheese share the word for sheep, so to say the name has nothing to do with the cheese overstates; the wine's being no relation of the cheese is all a guest needs.

traps[2]: "Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is the grape of Abruzzo, never Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, the Sangiovese of the Tuscan town."; now "Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is named for its grape; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is the Sangiovese of the Tuscan town.": Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is the wine and Montepulciano the grape; the trap had called the wine a grape.
open: The age past which an old bottle is decanted: the house's English page says more than twenty years, its home page that the wait was lengthened from ten years to twenty, and a 2016 profile that the Riserva has been decanted since 1997; the record gives no figure.
The founder's birthday on the day before his death is the author's reading of Sky TG24 and Gambero Rosso; the refuter's searches did not show it, so it is out until two sources show it.

records.place: San Martino sulla Marrucina, province of Chieti, Abruzzo

wine.name: Villa Gemma Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva
wine.classification: Riserva, the longer aged type of the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, by the house's sheets.
wine.sites: Colle Cave at San Martino sulla Marrucina, about 400 metres up in the hills of Chieti, on clay with limestone and facing south east; the vines are trained on Guyot in close rows rather than on the old pergola.
wine.making: Since 2012 it has fermented in stainless steel, in wood before, by the house's sheets, with twenty to thirty days on its skins; it then ages twelve to eighteen months by vintage in new or first fill French oak barriques and rests at least two years in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black plum and liquorice over mocha and vanilla from the new oak; full bodied and dense, with ripe, soft tannin, moderate acidity and a warm finish.
wine.ageing: The house holds it back until it is ready to drink, and it then gains savoury notes for many years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, in a large Bordeaux glass, after an hour in a decanter when the bottle is young.

label.means: The house's leading line of wines, a name first given to the red of 1984.
The DOC's longer aged type; Villa Gemma rests for years in barrel and bottle before release.
The region's red DOC, from the Montepulciano grape, not the Tuscan town.

records.table: French barriques, then years in bottle, shape Masciarelli's Villa Gemma Riserva, a Montepulciano d'Abruzzo of the Colle Cave hillside at San Martino sulla Marrucina. Black plum, liquorice and mocha in a dense, polished frame make it the grape's modern face, and a decanter readies it for roast meat.
records.story: His maternal grandfather, in the house's telling, gave Gianni Masciarelli, who died in 2008, his love of the vine, and in 1981 he founded his own estate at San Martino sulla Marrucina in the hills of Chieti; its first vintage gave some 700 bottles of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and 1,300 of Trebbiano d'Abruzzo. At a time when most of Abruzzo's wine left the region in bulk, he set out to give the native grapes a polish that would carry them abroad: close planted vines on Guyot beside the old pergola, and French barriques for the leading wines. With the 1984 vintage he made the first Villa Gemma, a Montepulciano from San Martino, and it became the wine through which the house found its style. In 1987 he met the partner of his life and work, and by the house's account their partnership gave the estate its reach abroad. On 31 July 2008 he died suddenly in Munich, and his partner took the estate on. Opposite Valentini and Pepe stands Villa Gemma, the other pole of Abruzzo: Montepulciano ripened, oaked and polished for the tables of the world.

others.name: Villa Gemma Cerasuolo
others.note: The line's Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo Superiore, of Montepulciano from vines on the traditional Abruzzo pergola, first made in 1986.

others.name: Villa Gemma Bianco
others.note: The line's white of Trebbiano, Cococciola and Pecorino, once sold as Colline Teatine IGT and as Abruzzo Bianco DOC by the 2024 vintage.

traps: Villa Gemma comes in three colours, a red Riserva, a Cerasuolo and a white; the flagship is the red Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva.
Masciarelli is the modern pole of Abruzzo, French barriques and ripe fruit, the opposite of Pepe's cement and Valentini's large old casks.

cards.front: Masciarelli's Villa Gemma Riserva: which vineyard gives it, and how are its vines trained?
cards.back: Colle Cave at San Martino sulla Marrucina, about 400 metres up, on Guyot in close rows rather than pergola.

cards.front: By Masciarelli's own account, who gave its founder his love of the vine?
cards.back: His maternal grandfather; the founder started his own estate at San Martino sulla Marrucina in 1981.

questions.q: A guest compares Masciarelli's Villa Gemma Riserva with Emidio Pepe's Montepulciano and asks where its vanilla and mocha come from. What is the source?
opts: Ageing in French oak barriques
Fermentation in glass lined cement
Years in large old Slavonian casks
Grapes dried on mats before pressing
questions.exp: Villa Gemma ages twelve to eighteen months in new or first fill French barriques; Pepe's red sees only cement, and large old casks give little vanilla.

questions.q: With the 1984 vintage, three years after founding Masciarelli, what did its founder first bottle as Villa Gemma?
opts: A Montepulciano red from San Martino
A barrel fermented Trebbiano
A Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo rosato
A sparkling Pecorino
questions.exp: By the house's sheets the first Villa Gemma, of 1984, was a Montepulciano from San Martino sulla Marrucina; the line's white and rosato are not the wine first made under the name.

report: Searches for this record: 5 in the author's first run and 2 in the second run's read-through.

The plan's note is answered in part: Gianni Masciarelli died on 31 July 2008 in Munich (Decanter, WineNews), but Decanter and WineNews give his age as 53 and a Japanese magazine (precious.jp), a forum and a travel site 52, and no source of either run gives a birth year, so he carries his death alone.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Marina Cvetic, his partner, and Miriam Lee Masciarelli, his daughter; the library's holdings line and two of its wines (Marina Cvetic Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva and Trebbiano d'Abruzzo Marina Cvetic) carry her name, so this record leaves those wines out of others and the library may wish to look again.
Library tension: p-masciarelli's first trap names Abruzzo's DOCGs as Colline Teramane and Tullum, while the region record adds Casauria, recognised in 2025, so the trap may be out of date.

The label: the house's sheets print Villa Gemma Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC Riserva (the 2018 vintage); the region record says that from the 2023 harvest Riserva is reserved for wines of the sub-zones, so later vintages may add a sub-zone name, which this record does not print.

The barrique time differs by sheet, twelve months in first passage barriques on the English sheet and eighteen in new ones on the Italian sheet of 2018, hence twelve to eighteen months by vintage; the first vintage of 1984 is on the house's sheets and in Decanter.

Left out: the Gambero Rosso guide's naming of the 1995 as the wine of the year of Italy in 2000 (an award and a ranking), the meaning of the name Villa Gemma (not found), the year the house took on the Castello di Semivicoli (not found), and a start at his father's winery in 1978 (one source).

Others, second run: La Botte di Gianni is taken out, since the house's own pages disagree on it (a Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva of 2010 from a 700 litre barrel on one sheet, a Trebbiano d'Abruzzo Riserva of 2010 from an old cask on another). The Cerasuolo's pergola and first vintage of 1986 are on the house's Villa Gemma Cerasuolo sheet (masciarelli.it/en/i-vini/villa-gemma-cerasuolo-dabruzzo-doc-superiore), the Bianco's grapes, its older Colline Teatine IGT and its Abruzzo Bianco DOC of 2024 on the house's store and Villa Gemma line pages; the Bianco is pergola and Guyot, so pergola trained is gone from its note. The story's partner and daughter is now the partner alone, as the library holds it; Vintus also says she took over in 2008.

changed: wine.making: "By the house's sheets it ferments in stainless steel with twenty to thirty days on its skins,"; now "By the house's sheets it has fermented in stainless steel since 2012, in wood before, with twenty to thirty days on its skins,": the house's Italian sheet of 2019 gives fermentation in wood until 2012 and in steel since, with twenty to thirty days of maceration, and the house's wine page notes the change of 2012; older bottles on a list were fermented in wood.

story: "On 31 July 2008 he died suddenly on a business trip to Munich,"; now "On 31 July 2008 he died suddenly in Munich,": WineNews says he died suddenly during a visit to Munich and Wine Spectator in a clinic there after a cerebral haemorrhage; no source of the refuter's says the journey was for business.

sources[1]: "Masciarelli Store: Villa Gemma Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC Riserva 2018"; now "Masciarelli: Villa Gemma Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva, scheda tecnica" (masciarelli.it, 2019): the house's Italian sheet carries the steel since 2012, the twenty to thirty days on the skins, the eighteen months in new barriques and the two years and more in bottle, which the store page of 2018 gave only in part.
open: A page in the refuter's results says Villa Gemma is named for the house where the founder grew up and was the first Riserva red of Abruzzo; one source, a claim of a first, so both stay out.
His age at death is 53 in WineNews and Decanter (the author's reading) and two other pages, and 52 in Wine Spectator; no birth year is in two sources, so he keeps his death alone.
The region record says Riserva is reserved for the sub-zones from the 2023 harvest; a Villa Gemma of a later vintage may print a sub-zone, which the record does not.

records.place: Controguerra, province of Teramo, Colline Teramane DOCG, Abruzzo

wine.name: Zanna Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane Riserva
wine.classification: DOCG by decree of 20 February 2003, the guaranteed designation of the Teramo hills
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, from the estate's Zanna vineyard.
wine.sites: The Zanna vineyard at Controguerra, the estate's first historic plot, at about 280 metres on dense, poorly porous soil of marl and clay; its name, the house says, recalls the wolves that once roamed there.
wine.making: Destemmed and crushed, the grapes ferment in stainless steel at no more than 30 degrees Celsius. After the malolactic the wine moves to casks of Slavonian oak of about 25 hectolitres for 24 to 26 months, then rests in bottle and is released only after the three years of ageing the DOCG asks of a Riserva; it is made only in the vintages the house judges right.
wine.glass: Plum, blackberry and liquorice over tar and a dusty note of the cask; full bodied and firm, its ripe tannin carrying a long, dark finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and dark on release, after years at the house, it opens over several more in bottle and keeps for many after that.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle one to two hours before it is poured; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The DOCG of the hills of Teramo province, granted in 2003, for Montepulciano.
Under the DOCG, at least three years of ageing before the wine is released.
The vineyard at Controguerra the family bought in 1960, named, the house says, for wolves.

records.table: Bought by the family in 1960, the vineyard at Controguerra gives Illuminati's Zanna, a Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane Riserva aged two years in large Slavonian oak casks and then in bottle. Plum, blackberry, liquorice and tar rest on firm tannin; roast lamb suits it after a decanting.
records.story: Fattoria Nicò was the name the founder gave the winery he opened in 1890 at Ripatransone, in the Marche just across the border from Abruzzo, and the house dates itself from it. In 1960 his grandson, Dino Illuminati, crossed to the Abruzzo side of the hills, to Controguerra in the province of Teramo, and bought a farmhouse and its land in a place called Zanna, a name the house links to the wolves that once roamed there. There he worked for the appellations of his hills: the Controguerra DOC and then the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG, granted by decree of 20 February 2003, the DOCG of the Teramo hills. The Zanna vineyard, his first plot there, gives the house's long aged Riserva, made only in the vintages it judges right. Dino Illuminati died in February 2023, at 92, and the family kept the estate going, five generations from the founder by the house's count. Zanna puts a face to the Colline Teramane: Montepulciano of the northern hills, aged in large casks and built to keep.

traps: Zanna is a vineyard and a wine, not a sub-zone: the appellation on the label is Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG.

report: Searches for this record: 8 in the author's first run, one of them empty on illuminativini.it before the house's domain was found to be illuminativini.com, and 3 in the second run's read-through.

The house began at Ripatransone in the Marche in 1890 as Fattoria Nicò and has been at Controguerra since 1960, by its own history page; the plan's why and the region record's producers line call it a Controguerra house of 1890, true of the house but not of the place.

The founder is described rather than named: no source gives his dates, and the house says a living descendant of five generations on bears the same name. Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Nicola Illuminati (the living one), Stefano Illuminati and Lorenzo Illuminati.

Dino Illuminati died at home at 92 (Gambero Rosso's obituary of 15 February 2023; Doctor Wine), and his birth year, 1930 or 1931, is in neither, so he carries his death alone; Gambero Rosso says he took the estate on in the 1950s and the house says he moved to Controguerra in 1960, so the record keeps 1960.

The plan calls the house a founder of the Colline Teramane DOCG; Gambero Rosso calls Dino Illuminati an early champion of the Controguerra DOC and the Colline Teramane DOCG, and a guide (Vinoscout) says he fought for the Controguerra DOC of 1996, so the story says he worked for both and gives no year for the DOC.

Left out: Zanna's first vintage (not found in either run), tendone training at about 1,100 vines a hectare (one sales sheet), the house's vineyard size (volatile and in conflict, 110 or 130 hectares), and Gambero Rosso's line that Dino Illuminati was among the first to bottle Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (one source, a claim of a first). The house's history page calls him the founder's grandson; one merchant says nephew, a reading of the Italian nipote, and the record follows the house.

The marl and clay, the steel at no more than 30 degrees, the casks of about 25 hectolitres for 24 to 26 months and the two years in bottle are on the house's Zanna page; Slavonian oak and the vintages only it judges right are on its English page and two merchants' (Superiore.de, Bottle of Italy). Pieluni as a Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane Riserva DOCG is on two merchants' pages (Superiore.de, Bottle of Italy) and the house's Reserve list.

story: "Dino Illuminati died at home in February 2023, at 92,"; now "Dino Illuminati died in February 2023, at 92,": AbruzzoWeb says he died at San Benedetto del Tronto after a short illness, and no source of the refuter's says at home; the month and the age stand on AbruzzoWeb, Il Messaggero, Il Centro and Virtù Quotidiane.

AbruzzoWeb and Il Centro report that Dino Illuminati was the first president of the Colline Teramane consortium and the man behind Abruzzo's first DOCG, and that he was made a Cavaliere del Lavoro in 2005; the refuter read them in one search summary and did not add them.
Zanna's first vintage is still in no source; the plan's note asks for it.

records.place: Ofena, province of L'Aquila, Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC, Abruzzo

wine.name: Piè delle Vigne Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
wine.classification: DOC, Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo's own since 2010, before that a type of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
wine.grapes: Montepulciano alone, from the house's vineyards at Ofena.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards around Ofena, between about 320 and 440 metres, in a small plateau shaped like an amphitheatre under the Gran Sasso that locals call the Forno d'Abruzzo, the oven of Abruzzo.
wine.making: The house describes its making as svacata, an old step of the farmhouse cellars: part of the Montepulciano ferments as a white wine, off its skins, and part as a red, and about halfway through the fermentation the red is drawn off its skins and joined to the white. It then spends a year in stainless steel and a year in bottle.
wine.glass: Deep cherry red; wild raspberry, sour cherry and red cherry with almond and a stony note; dry and vinous, with fresh acidity, a light grip of tannin and almond bitterness at the close.
wine.ageing: Bottled a year before it is sold, it is ready at once and keeps its fruit, gaining depth, for a few years more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, cooler than a red and warmer than a pale rosé; decanting adds nothing; a white wine glass.

label.means: Abruzzo's DOC for rosato of Montepulciano, named for its cherry colour; its own DOC since 2010.
Italian for the foot of the vines, the name given to this Cerasuolo, first made in 1997.

records.table: Under the Gran Sasso at Ofena, Cataldi Madonna makes Piè delle Vigne by the old svacata method, part of a red fermentation joined to a white: a Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo of Montepulciano. Deep cherry red in the glass, with wild raspberry and almond, it is served cool.
records.story: Work with the vine at Ofena began in 1920 under a baron of the family, as the house records it, and it was his son who first bottled wine under the family name, in 1975. Since that year the labels have carried the Warrior of Capestrano, the ancient stone statue found near the vineyards. In 1988 the bottler's son, a professor of philosophy at L'Aquila, made the Montepulciano Tonì in his father's honour; he took over in 1990 and died in December 2025. Ofena lies in the small basin that locals call the oven of Abruzzo, under the Gran Sasso. With the 1997 vintage the house first made Piè delle Vigne by svacata, an old step of the farmhouse cellars in which part of the must is drawn off a red fermentation halfway through and joined to a white one. Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo, from 1968 a type of the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC, became a DOC of its own in 2010, and the house's grapes have been certified organic since 2016, by its account. Pour Piè delle Vigne for a guest who thinks rosé a light summer wine: Cerasuolo is cherry coloured and vinous, made for food.

report: Searches for this record: 5 in the author's first run and 2 in the second run's read-through; the house's pages were read through search.

The pick: no page of the house names one wine its flagship; Gambero Rosso's guide Vini d'Italia 2021 made the Piè delle Vigne 2018 its rosato of the year (an award, not used in prose), so the pick is kept as the group's rosato, with Tonì and the Pecorino Giulia under others.

The label: the house's shop and Falstaff print the 2024 vintage as Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo Superiore Terre Aquilane DOC, while older vintages read Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC, so the record prints Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo alone; the region record names the L'Aquila sub-zone Terre de L'Aquila, where the ministry's single document and the label read Terre Aquilane.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Giulia Cataldi Madonna (the refuter found that Luigi Cataldi Madonna, the son who made Tonì in 1988 and took over in 1990, died on 8 December 2025, so he is not for people.json); the baron of 1920, also Luigi Cataldi Madonna, and his son Antonio, who first bottled in 1975, are described, for no source gives their dates.

The relationship: the house's Tonì page (cataldimadonna.com/shop/montepulciano-d-abruzzo-toni) says it was made in honour of the maker's father Tonino and ties it to 1988, without saying plainly whether 1988 is its first vintage or the year it was named, and its history says Antonio first bottled in 1975, so the record calls the man of 1988 the bottler's son; one search summary called him Antonio's nephew, a reading of the Italian nipote, and the refuter may wish to confirm. The Tonì page gives barriques until 2015 and the 25 hectolitre cask from 2017; the Giulia and Supergiulia pages (shop/pecorino-giulia, shop/pecorino-igt-supergiulia) give IGT Terre d'Abruzzo and the double selection. Those three pages are not in the sources for the cap of five.

The svacata is the house's account, with Gazzetta del Gusto's interview (part of the must drawn off about halfway through fermentation, first tried in 1997) as the second; a merchant's account of two pickings, about 85 and 15 per cent, and a maceration of four to five days are left out.

Region record tension: its producers line calls the estate the reference estate of Ofena on the high L'Aquila plateau, a word of judgement; the house puts its vines at 320 to 440 metres in a basin, which the record follows. The house's claim that the Calderone above it is the only glacier of the Apennines is left out.
Cerasuolo as a type of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from 1968 is in the consorzio's disciplinare, and its own DOC by decree of 5 October 2010 in the European Union's eAmbrosia file.

changed: story: "In 1988 the bottler's son made the Montepulciano Tonì in his father's honour, and in 1990 he took the estate on."; now "In 1988 the bottler's son, a professor of philosophy at L'Aquila, made the Montepulciano Tonì in his father's honour; he took the estate on in 1990 and died in December 2025.": Luigi Cataldi Madonna, whom the author believed living, died on 8 December 2025 at 69 (Askanews, Il Centro, AbruzzoLive, Gambero Rosso); Gambero Rosso gives him the estate from his father Antonio around 1990 and the founding to his grandfather the baron, which bears out the bottler's son and the honour to his father, and the obituaries give his chair in the history of philosophy at the University of L'Aquila. He stays described, not named, for his birth year is in Gambero Rosso alone.

others[1].note: "The house's Pecorino, sold as IGT Terre d'Abruzzo;"; now "The house's Pecorino, an IGT labelled Terre Aquilane or Terre d'Abruzzo by vintage;": Falstaff and the house's shop print the 2024 Giulia as Terre d'Abruzzo IGT, while Italy's Finest Wines, Viaswine and two shops print Giulia and Supergiulia of earlier vintages as IGT Terre Aquilane.

open: Italy's Finest Wines calls Tonì the flagship of the house; the pick keeps Piè delle Vigne as the group's rosato, as the plan's note intends.
One merchant's page says the 2007 was the first Piè delle Vigne made without wood; one source, left out of the making.
The askanews summary says the late son handed the running of the estate to his daughter in 2019; one source, left out, and the daughter is living.
